title: Why Transformers Struggle with Distribution-Independent In-Context Learning
claim: Models that are near-perfect in distribution degrade sharply as test distribution shifts, while an explicit least-squares baseline stays at zero error.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots sharing one top legend, left-to-right, dotted baseline
description: Two line plots sit side by side under a shared legend. The legend maps six polynomial degrees (Deg 1 to Deg 6) to colored markers: blue circle, orange square, green triangle, pink diamond, yellow inverted triangle and black star. It also shows a solid line for the Transformer model and a dotted line for the least-squares (LS) baseline. Panel (a) plots MSE against the shift scale sigma from 1 to 10. Every degree's curve rises convexly from near zero to about 27–38, with a gray shaded band around the black Deg 6 curve. Panel (b) plots normalized MSE on the same x-axis. The curves rise and flatten out between about 0.53 and 0.68, and the degrees split into visible groups. In both panels the LS dotted lines lie flat at zero along the x-axis. Shaded bands show standard deviation.
caption: Mean squared error (MSE; left) and normalized MSE (NMSE; right) under distribution shift. Each Transformer (12 layers, 8 attention heads, $d_{\mathrm{emb}}=256$) is trained and evaluated on a single polynomial degree from 1 to 6. Training inputs and coefficients are sampled from $\mathcal{U}(-1,1)$. At test time, inputs follow the same distribution, while coefficients are sampled from $\mathcal{U}(-\sigma,\sigma)$. Solid curves show Transformer results, and dotted curves show least-squares baselines. Results are averaged over five evaluation seeds; shaded regions indicate $\pm$ one standard deviation. The evaluation protocol is described in Appendix [ref].
abstract: With in-context learning (ICL), transformer models adapt to new tasks from illustrative examples at inference time without updating their parameters. A common interpretation is that transformers implement implicit learning algorithms in their forward pass. We test this interpretation and ICL capability under distribution shift in noiseless polynomial regression, where the context uniquely determines the target function. Models that are near-perfect in distribution exhibit sharp performance degradation under shifts in the input or target-function distribution. This behavior persists across polynomial degrees and multiple training interventions, and in higher-dimensional nonlinear regression. We identify two architectural mechanisms that explain this breakdown: output saturation at finite boundary values linked to final normalization, and attention concentration on a small subset of the context, which can limit context-dependent adaptation required for ICL. Controlled experiments, architectural ablations, targeted interventions, and theoretical analysis provide strong evidence for both mechanisms and their consequence: strong in-distribution ICL does not imply distribution-independent ICL, which calls for caution when using ICL instead of explicit retraining or adaptation under distribution shift.
